newsitem.title: USA: Dining-out gene shows up in fruit flies - research.
newsitem.headline: Dining-out gene shows up in fruit flies - research.

text.p: Do you adore dining out, far from the reach of home cooking? The reason could be genetic, especially if you happen to be a fruit fly, researchers reported on Thursday.

A single gene appears to determine whether fruit flies -- and possibly mammals, including humans -- like to forage for food far away or prefer eating close to home, according to Marla Sokolowski, a biologist at York University in Toronto.
The fruit fly world is divided into two distinct types, rovers and sitters, Sokolowski and colleagues wrote in this week's edition of the journal Science.
Rovers are willing to travel farther for food than the sitters, but both types will roam if food supplies are scarce enough. And rovers will stay home to eat if conditions are right.
"You can make a rover eat at home by providing fantastic food," Sokolowski said in a telephone interview. Starving rovers just a bit helps keep them from straying too, she said.

The vast majority of fruit flies, 70 percent, are rovers, and the genetic basis of the trait means this is a true bimorphism: flies fall into one or the other category, with none who sometimes rove and sometimes sit.
Rovers can be turned into sitters only with genetic intervention or drastic measures such as application of gamma radiation, which causes the gene to mutate.
The chance that humans have a similar gene is quite good, Sokolowski said.
The gene in fruit flies triggers production of a brain enzyme, and mice and humans have been shown to have the same brain enzyme.

Rover flies have more of this enzyme than sitters do, but it has been difficult to study the role it may play in the feeding habits of humans because the levels of the enzyme in human brains are low, Sokolowski said.
But she noted that many other genes first discovered in fruit flies have shed light on human biology.

"There's reason to think that this (enzyme) may have a similar function in humans," Sokolowski said. "Whether or not it plays a role in regulation of feeding in humans? I think there is a possibility for that."
One possible next step would be for researchers to study humans with eating disorders to see whether they have different levels of this brain enzyme than normal humans, Sokolowski said.
